title: Multi-Level Caches
summary: Why CPUs stack L1, L2, and L3, and the inclusion policy that governs what each level is allowed to hold.

slides.subTitle: Fast and large don't mix
slides.markdown:
One cache can't be both very fast and very large — larger SRAM arrays have longer wire delays and need more pipeline stages to search, so bigger inherently means slower. Instead of picking one compromise size, CPUs stack **several** cache levels, each larger and slower than the last.

The closest level (L1) stays small enough to answer in a cycle or two; each level behind it trades a bit more latency for a lot more capacity, so most accesses still resolve quickly while the working set as a whole still fits somewhere fast.

slides.subTitle: Smallest, fastest, per-core
slides.markdown:
**L1** is the smallest and fastest level, typically 32–64 KB, answering in 1–4 cycles, and private to each core. It's almost always **split** into an instruction cache (I-cache) and a data cache (D-cache), so instruction fetch and data access don't contend for the same ports and structure.

Being this close to the pipeline means L1 must be small — its size is set by how much SRAM can be searched within a single cycle's timing budget, not by how much programs would like to fit there.

slides.subTitle: Bigger, still usually per-core
slides.markdown:
**L2** sits behind L1, typically 256 KB–2 MB, answering in roughly 10–20 cycles. It's usually still private per core (though some designs share it across a small cluster) and unified — one cache for both instructions and data, rather than split like L1.

L2 exists to catch the working set that L1 is simply too small to hold, at a latency still far cheaper than going all the way to L3 or RAM.

slides.subTitle: Shared, largest, closest to memory
slides.markdown:
**L3** is shared across all cores on a chip, typically several to tens of MB, answering in 30–70 cycles — noticeably slower than L2 but still far faster than RAM's 100+ cycles. Being shared lets it flexibly serve whichever core needs capacity most, and gives cores a fast way to see data another core recently touched, without going all the way to memory.

This is also the level most tied up in cache coherence traffic between cores, since it's the natural meeting point before memory.

slides.subTitle: Sizes and latencies at a glance
slides.markdown:
Stacking the levels together shows the full trade-off curve.

![The L1/L2/L3/memory hierarchy with typical sizes and latencies per level](assets/multi-level-hierarchy.svg)

Each level is roughly an order of magnitude larger and several times slower than the one above it — L1 to RAM spans a difference of over 100x in size and roughly 100x in latency.

slides.subTitle: Inclusion policy
slides.markdown:
**Inclusive**: every line in L1 must also exist in L2 (and L2's contents in L3). **Exclusive**: a line lives in exactly one level at a time — never duplicated. **Non-inclusive**: no guarantee either way; a line in L1 may or may not also be in L2.

This choice isn't cosmetic — it directly determines how much a lower level's capacity is "wasted" holding duplicates, and how simple or costly cache coherence tracking becomes, as the next slide covers.

slides.subTitle: Capacity waste vs coherence simplicity
slides.markdown:
| Policy | Effective total capacity | Coherence tracking |
|---|---|---|
| Inclusive | Reduced — L3 wastes space duplicating everything already in L1/L2 | Simple — L3 alone can tell whether any core might hold a line, no need to snoop L1/L2 directly |
| Exclusive | Full — every byte of SRAM holds unique data | Harder — a coherence check may need to look in any level, since there's no guaranteed duplicate at the outer level |

**How to decide:** inclusive designs accept wasted capacity in exchange for a single, fast place to answer "does any core have this line cached?" — valuable as core counts grow and coherence traffic gets expensive. Exclusive designs prioritize using every byte of SRAM, common when total cache capacity is at more of a premium than coherence-check simplicity.

slides.subTitle: Back-invalidation
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Inclusive just means L3 keeps a copy of everything — it can't hurt L1/L2, since they still have their own copy too."

**Why it's wrong:** when L3 needs to evict a line to make room, an inclusive design must also **invalidate that same line in every L1/L2 that holds it** — otherwise L3's invariant ("if it's in L1/L2, it's in L3") breaks. This is **back-invalidation**, and it can evict a line from L1 that core is still actively using, purely because L3 ran out of room for an unrelated reason.

**Correct model:** inclusion isn't free capacity waste alone — it couples L1/L2's residency to L3's eviction decisions, occasionally forcing out hot inner-level data the inner level itself would never have chosen to evict.

slides.subTitle: The noisy-neighbor problem
slides.markdown:
Because L3 is shared across all cores, one core running a cache-hungry workload (a large scan, say) can evict another core's hot working set purely by consuming shared capacity — the two workloads may be completely unrelated in code, yet compete for the same physical L3 space. This is the cache-level version of a noisy-neighbor problem, and it's a real source of unpredictable tail latency on shared, multi-tenant hosts.

Hardware mitigations exist for exactly this: **cache partitioning** (e.g. Intel's Cache Allocation Technology) lets software reserve a fixed slice of L3 ways for a given core or process, so a noisy workload can't evict a latency-sensitive one's data no matter how aggressively it scans.
